paras: The Musick's Ferry mob attack on Franz Suppenbach took place in mid-July 1882 at Musick's Ferry, St. Louis County, Missouri, when a crowd of Black men went at night to the house of a German laborer who was living with a Black woman. The German fired a musket into the crowd, and first wire reports said he had killed a preacher and was then drowned or hanged by the mob. Corrections a week later said that no one had died and that the man, named in them as Franz Suppenbach, had walked to St. Louis with the woman.

According to the Illinois Staats-Zeitung, which cited the 'W. P.', Suppenbach was a recent German immigrant who found work in February on the farm of Louis Harder, where a Black man named Robert Norris also worked. Through Norris he met Norris's widowed sister, Louisa Umble, a mother of four, and the two came to live as man and wife. The wire dispatches called him Henry Francis and said the Black people of the neighborhood were 'scandallized' that he was living with an unmarried woman and set out to 'regulate matters'.
The German paper reported that the neighbors held an open-air indignation meeting at which the colored schoolteacher Lee and Robert Norris spoke and the gathering resolved to punish the German.

The St. Louis dispatch said Rev. Columbus Lee, George Morris and thirty other men went to the house on Saturday night 'to lynch him', while a National Associated Press dispatch dated July 17 placed the attack on 'last night'. In the later accounts the crowd meant to flog him, tar and feather him and drive him from the country; according to the Staats-Zeitung they broke open the door and dragged the woman out of the house. When they came back for him, he fired an old musket at them about midnight, and the Milan Exchange added that the widow resisted with a razor.

The first dispatches said the shot killed the preacher and fatally wounded Morris (or 'Merris'), and that the crowd took the German at daylight and drowned him in the Missouri River; the Omaha Daily Bee's version said he was taken away and 'supposed' hanged. The Staats-Zeitung instead said the charge tore the flesh of Lee's right forearm and struck Norris in the left shoulder and cheek, and that the crowd fled.

The next morning, according to the Staats-Zeitung, the woman left her children with a friend and walked with Suppenbach to St. Louis, where the couple were seen in the northern part of the city that evening. The paper said neither Lee's nor Norris's wound was dangerous, and no report of an arrest or inquest appears in the coverage.

The story spread by wire on July 17 and 18 under headlines such as 'Scandal in Colored Circles', 'Lynching. Murder and Mysterious Disappearance' and 'Hanged by a Negro Mob', and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union reduced it to one line saying Francis 'was then drowned by the mob'.

Several papers treated the Black crowd with irony: the St. Paul Daily Globe headed the item 'Virtuous Indignation by Gentlemen of Color', and the Milan Exchange called the attackers 'moralists' and 'regulators' who 'retired in bad order'. The corrected version appeared in the Milan Exchange on July 22 and in German in the Illinois Staats-Zeitung on July 24; no retraction appears in the coverage from the papers that had carried the death reports.

The accounts disagree on the German's fate (drowned, hanged, or alive in St. Louis), on whether the preacher died, and on names, with the later, more detailed accounts reporting no deaths. They also differ on the crowd's aim: the St. Louis dispatch said it came to lynch him, while the corrections describe a plan to flog and tar and feather him and drive him away.

bases: A crowd of Black men attacked the house of a white German laborer over his relationship with a Black woman, broke in and dragged her out, and were driven off by his gunfire; the first reports that he was drowned or hanged were contradicted by later accounts (A1, A2, A15, A16).

First-day wire reports said a preacher was killed and Francis drowned or hanged (A1, A2, A4), while two later accounts say the attackers were only wounded and the German was alive in St. Louis (A15, A16).

accounts.label: Chicago/Musick's Ferry special
accounts.gist: Scandalized Black men surrounded the house about midnight; Francis fired, killing a preacher and probably fatally wounding Merris/Morris; the crowd was reported to have drowned him in the Missouri at daylight.

accounts.label: St. Louis dispatch
accounts.gist: Lee, Morris and thirty others went Saturday night to lynch Francis; he killed Lee and fatally wounded Morris and was believed drowned.

accounts.label: National Associated Press
accounts.gist: A mob headed by Rev. Columbus Lill waited on Francis; he killed Lill and mortally wounded Morris, and was taken away and supposed hanged.

accounts.label: Later corrections
accounts.gist: The crowd meant to flog or tar and feather Suppenbach and drive him off; he and the woman resisted, two attackers were wounded, none killed, and the couple went to St. Louis.

framing.detail: The first-day dispatches ran under sensational headlines such as 'Hanged by a Negro Mob' and 'Lynching. Murder and Mysterious Disappearance', presenting the drowning as a report.
The St. Paul Daily Globe and the Milan Exchange treated the Black attackers ironically ('Virtuous Indignation by Gentlemen of Color', 'moralists', 'regulators').
